Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

vignette:
You are a 41-year-old married man, a dancer of Middle Eastern descent, and you are sitting in my office because you can no longer pretend the past is not inside your body. Your name is Karim. You grew up in a city that became a war zone, and you carry that city with you in ways you never expected.

The day the shelling began, you were walking home from rehearsal. The air smelled of dry earth and something metallic, a smell you now catch in the soil of a potted plant or on a windy afternoon. You heard the whistle of the first mortar, then the crack, then the screaming. You ran, but you could not outrun the sound. That sound—a low, percussive thud followed by a high, tearing ring—is still with you. It comes back when a door slams, when a truck rumbles past your apartment, when someone drops a heavy box in the hallway. Each time, your chest locks, your breath shortens, and you feel the same helplessness you felt that day.

Over the months that followed, you began to notice something else. When you heard a sound that reminded you of the shelling, you felt not only fear but a hollow, dead feeling inside—as if the fear had burned out and left only ash. You told me, "I feel dead inside." That numbness has become a kind of constant companion, a gray fog that settles over everything. You have also lost your faith in people. Before the war, you believed in community, in the kindness of strangers. Now, when you hear a name that reminds you of someone who died—a name like "Tariq" or "Layla"—you feel a wave of bitterness, a certainty that the world is cruel and that others can see what happened to you just by looking at you. You are convinced that people can read the trauma on your face, that they know you are broken. This belief grows stronger each time you are triggered. The sounds and smells and names do not just remind you of the war; they confirm your worst appraisals of yourself and the world.

Your work as a dancer has become almost impossible. You teach at a studio where the floors are sprung, the mirrors are tall, and the music is loud. But the loud music—especially the sudden percussion in a contemporary piece—can sound too much like the shelling. You have started to avoid certain rehearsals, claiming minor injuries. You have stopped taking on solo performances because you fear that during a quiet moment on stage, a sound from the street or a dropped prop will send you into a freeze. Your wife has noticed you pulling away. She asks why you no longer dance at home, why you flinch when she claps her hands to get your attention. You do not tell her that the sound of her clapping reminds you of the mortar that landed three blocks from your childhood home.

The cycle tightens. A trigger—a smell of dry earth, a sudden loud noise, a name overheard in a café—brings on the numbness and the lost faith. And those appraisals, in turn, make you more vigilant, more watchful for the next trigger. You scan every room for potential sounds, every conversation for names that might undo you. You have come to believe that you are permanently damaged, that others can see it, and that there is no point in trying to reconnect. What finally brought you here was a moment in the studio last week: a dancer dropped a metal water bottle, and you dropped to the floor, covering your head, in front of twenty students. The shame was immediate and total. You are afraid that you will lose your career and your marriage. But what frightens you most is the thought that this deadness inside you is all that is left. You are hoping, I think, that I can help you find a way to feel alive again, even if you are not sure that is possible.
